passages.heading: Description
passages.source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.says: Helium is the one liquid that cooling alone does not freeze: at ordinary pressure it stays liquid down to absolute zero, and raising the pressure solidifies it readily.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.says: A fluorine compound was first recorded in use around 1670, in instructions for etching glass with Bohemian emerald (CaF2).

passages.heading: History
passages.source: IUPAC Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights (CIAAW)
passages.says: Carl-Wilhelm Scheele found fluorine in hydrofluoric acid in 1771, and Henri Moissan first isolated it in 1886.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.says: Alum served the ancient Greeks and Romans as an astringent and, in dyeing, as a mordant.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: IUPAC Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights (CIAAW)
passages.says: Impure aluminium was first isolated in 1825, by Hans Christian Oersted, a Danish physicist.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: IUPAC Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights (CIAAW)
passages.says: Jöns Jacob Berzelius found silicon, in its amorphous form, in 1824, and Henri Sainte-Claire Deville first made the crystalline form in 1854.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.says: The Romans made lime, which they called calx, in the first century, but the metal was found only in 1808.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.says: Humphry Davy first isolated calcium metal in 1808, by electrolysing lime (CaO) mixed with mercuric oxide (HgO).

passages.heading: Uses
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.says: At standard atmospheric pressure arsenic sublimes, passing from solid straight to gas at 887 K; it becomes liquid only under raised pressure, and under 28 times standard atmospheric pressure it melts, at 1090 K.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.says: The astatine made so far comes to 0.05 micrograms in all (0.00000005 g).

passages.heading: Uses
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.says: Astatine has been produced only in small amounts and is short-lived, so it has no use beyond basic research.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.says: No amount of francium large enough to weigh has been prepared or isolated.

passages.heading: Uses
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.says: Francium has been produced only in small amounts and is short-lived, so it has no use beyond basic research.

passages.heading: Description
passages.source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.says: Fermium is the heaviest element that bombarding lighter elements with neutrons can make, and so the heaviest of which a macroscopic amount can be prepared.

passages.heading: Description
passages.source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.says: No fermium metal has been prepared, though fermium alloyed with rare earth metals has been measured, and several predictions have been made.

passages.heading: Uses
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.says: Fermium has been produced only in small amounts and is short-lived, so it has no use beyond basic research.
